analyses.title: On-Line New Event Detection and Tracking
analyses.research_question: How can a system operating strictly online detect previously unseen real-world news events and continue tracking those events as their reporting and descriptive features evolve over time?
analyses.methodology: The paper evaluates online new-event detection and event tracking on the TDT pilot corpus, which contains broadcast-news and newswire stories with exhaustive judgments for 25 selected events. New-event detection is implemented as a single-pass clustering/classification process using weighted lexical queries, event-specific thresholds, and a time penalty, with miss and false-alarm tradeoffs evaluated by DET curves, leave-one-event-out parameter selection, and bootstrap estimation. Event tracking is evaluated with rolling per-event training sets of 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16 example stories, using tf-idf-style query representations, common and temporally surprising features, and an adaptive procedure that rebuilds a query when newly accepted stories appear. Failure analysis is used to examine event granularity and semantic drift.

key_findings.finding: The paper treats concrete event identity, rather than broad topical similarity, as the central relation for detection: a story is old if it describes an event identical to one already represented, and otherwise it is a new event.

The authors find that event identity is intrinsically difficult to delimit by time and place; their own examples show that an intuitively single event can extend across long periods and multiple locations.

Adding a temporal penalty to detection thresholds generally improved performance, supporting the idea that stories close together in the stream are more likely to concern the same event than stories far apart.

Failure analysis shows a granularity problem: representations of a specific event can drift toward a broad event class, causing a system to confuse distinct plane crashes, bombing-related stories, or other events that share class-level vocabulary.

Event tracking benefits substantially from incremental adaptation because important event-specific entities and facts may emerge only well after the initial stories; adaptive query rebuilding can capture such later features and reduce the amount of initial training material required.

The proposed 'surprising feature' heuristic does not by itself provide sufficiently reliable event coverage: some true event stories lack the surprising term, while some unusual terms are accidental or retrieval-useless.

The paper explicitly identifies the relationship between an event and a sub-event, and the appropriate level of event granularity, as unresolved research questions rather than solved relations in its model.
The suggestion that combining surprise with a feature's subsequent persistence will improve adaptive tracking is presented as a hypothesis rather than demonstrated experimentally in this paper.

limitations: The study uses broadcast news and newswire rather than enterprise email or organizational chat, so it is not direct evidence about cross-thread workplace communication.
The TDT pilot corpus is small by information-retrieval standards and contains only 25 judged events; the authors explicitly characterize the results as suggestive rather than conclusive.

The operational decision is largely binary same-event versus new-event, even though the paper recognizes ambiguity in event granularity; graded, partial, hierarchical, or non-transitive continuity relations are not explicitly modeled.
Event/sub-event structure is raised as future work rather than evaluated.
The surprising-feature formulation is described as largely ad hoc and does not obtain broad enough coverage for reliable tracking by itself.
Some tracking evaluations at larger training-set sizes necessarily cover fewer events because several judged events contain too few relevant stories.
The work predates modern semantic representations and relies mainly on lexical features, so failures from class-level lexical overlap are prominent.
raw_claims: New-event detection and event tracking are formulated as relationships among stories based on the real-world events the stories describe.
A new-event detector must decide on each arriving story before seeing any later story.
The authors distinguish specific event identity from membership in a broad event class.
They note that simple time-and-place definitions of an event fail for extended phenomena such as the O. J. Simpson saga.
The TDT pilot evaluation uses judged events in a mixed Reuters and CNN news stream.
The detection system uses story-derived lexical queries and event-specific thresholds within a single-pass online procedure.
A time penalty improves the thresholding model because recent stories are more likely to concern the same event.
Bootstrap evaluation with the selected detection parameters produced a mean miss rate of 40.5% and a mean false-alarm rate of 7.8%.
Failure cases show that generic vocabulary can make a query for one concrete event behave like a classifier for an entire event class.
Tracking experiments use progressively larger seed sets and evaluate later stories for the same event.
Common-word tracking queries need relatively few features, with the paper reporting little additional benefit from very large query representations.
Important event descriptors can appear only after many earlier stories, which motivates adaptive tracking.
Adaptive tracking rebuilds an event query after accepting a new relevant story so that later-emerging features can enter the representation.
The surprising-feature experiment shows that unusual terms can be event-indicative but can also have poor coverage or be accidental.
The conclusion leaves event-versus-subevent relationships and preferred event granularity as open problems.

analyses.title: Distance-aware Calibration for Pre-trained Language Models
analyses.research_question: Can a post-hoc calibration method that reduces confidence as a sample moves farther from the training distribution improve language-model calibration under distribution shift and improve out-of-distribution detection?
analyses.methodology: The authors propose Distance Aware Calibration (DAC), which uses the distance between a test sample's language-model embedding and the training-set embeddings to mix the model's predictive distribution toward a uniform distribution as distance increases. The default implementation uses deep k-nearest-neighbor distance over hidden representations and selects its calibration parameter through a multi-objective procedure balancing in-domain Expected Calibration Error and in-/out-of-domain discrimination measured by precision-recall area, with a knee-selection algorithm choosing the operating point. BERT-base and RoBERTa-base are evaluated against uncalibrated models, temperature scaling, and SNGP across synthetic character corruption, cross-dataset content shifts, and OOD-detection benchmarks. The paper also ablates the OOD calibration-set source and size and compares KNN distance with Mahalanobis and Gaussian-mixture alternatives.

key_findings.finding: DAC consistently improves out-of-distribution calibration over the evaluated baselines under random-character and keyboard-typo perturbations, with the largest gains at higher noise levels.
key_findings.section: 5.1 DAC improves OOD calibration under different domain-shifts

key_findings.finding: Under non-synthetic content shifts, DAC remains strong for OOD calibration but temperature scaling is a substantially stronger competitor and beats DAC in at least the RoBERTa natural-language-inference case.
key_findings.section: 5.1 DAC improves OOD calibration under different domain-shifts

key_findings.finding: For in-domain calibration, DAC improves on the uncalibrated model, but temperature scaling is generally more effective.
key_findings.section: 5.1 DAC improves OOD calibration under different domain-shifts

key_findings.finding: Using DAC confidence for OOD detection improves the underlying language model and achieves the best reported result among the compared methods in all but one evaluated model/task case.
key_findings.section: 5.2 DAC makes language models better OOD detectors

key_findings.finding: The ablation finds KNN distance more effective than Mahalanobis distance or a Gaussian-mixture-model score for DAC in the evaluated noisy-text settings.

DAC is not completely insensitive to its calibration data: its results vary with both the size and source of the OOD calibration set, and IMDB produces the weakest and most variable results in the reported comparison.

The paper provides no evidence about longitudinal conversation identity, enterprise email/chat linking, evolving work-item identity, subevents, or non-transitive continuity relations; its distance notion concerns statistical distance from a training distribution rather than continuity between messages or business events.

limitations: DAC requires access to the original training data, or at least precomputed representations of it, at inference time.
Training-sample embeddings must be precomputed and stored in an index, which can be expensive for very large training sets.
Calibration requires a small set of out-of-distribution examples.
Performance varies with the choice and size of the OOD calibration set despite the authors' robustness findings.
The experiments are limited to BERT-base and RoBERTa-base rather than a broad range of contemporary model families and scales.
The main calibration experiments use classification benchmarks and synthetic character corruptions, so they do not establish behavior for longitudinal enterprise communication.

The work does not study threads, conversations, work items, concrete organizational events, subevents, temporal continuation, or cross-thread linking; it is therefore methodologically peripheral to the stated literature-review topic.
A companion implementation of DAC itself is not identified in the paper, although the experiments use publicly available libraries and benchmark datasets.
raw_claims: DAC is a post-hoc method that adjusts each sample's confidence using its distance from the model's training data.
As distance from the training set increases, DAC moves the predictive distribution toward maximum uncertainty.
The default distance is computed with nearest neighbors over language-model hidden representations.
The calibration parameter is selected by jointly considering in-domain calibration error and discrimination between in-domain and OOD samples.
The experiments use base BERT and base RoBERTa models.
Synthetic distribution shifts include random character edits and keyboard-typo corruptions applied at several intensities.
The evaluation also includes content shifts between datasets for paraphrase detection and natural-language inference.
Calibration is evaluated with Expected Calibration Error, while OOD detection uses AUROC, PRAUC, and FPR95.
DAC gives especially large calibration improvements when character noise is substantial.
Temperature scaling is generally stronger than DAC for in-domain calibration, even though DAC is stronger in many OOD settings.
On the reported OOD-detection experiments, DAC improves the base model and leads the compared methods in all but one case.
For RoBERTa on the IMDB OOD-detection setting, DAC reports an AUROC of 90.18 compared with 87.85 for SNGP and 81.34 for the uncalibrated model.
The OOD source used during calibration affects DAC's variance and final calibration quality.
KNN distance performs better than the tested Mahalanobis and Gaussian-mixture alternatives.
The method requires retained training representations and some OOD calibration examples.
